title: Columbus Olde Towne East Gets 65-Unit Affordable Project on E. Main
author: CREN Newsroom
excerpt: A Cincinnati developer proposes 65-unit Olde Towne East affordable housing at 907 East Main, backed by an OHFA tax credit and $3.25M in city HOME funds.

body:
Kingsley + Co., a Cincinnati developer founded by retired NFL player Chinedum Ndukwe, has won a state tax credit award for a proposed 65-unit affordable building at 907–917 East Main Street in Columbus's Olde Towne East. The $22.8 million project named Mercy on Main would be the firm's first low-income housing tax credit development in Columbus.

## The Developer's Path to Columbus

[Kingsley + Co.](https://www.kingsleyandcompany.com/post/kingsley-co-expands-affordable-housing-efforts-into-columbus-with-mercy-on-main) was founded by Chinedum Ndukwe after he retired from professional football in 2012. Ndukwe played for the Cincinnati Bengals and the Oakland Raiders following his time at the University of Notre Dame. The company has since built a track record in affordable housing development concentrated in Cincinnati, and Mercy on Main represents its third 9% LIHTC project overall — and the first time it has entered the Columbus market.

The project is named for Mercy Okoronkwo, Ndukwe's grandmother. The 907–917 East Main Street site is currently underused. The developer's plan calls for redeveloping the parcels into a five-story building with housing, parking, access roads, sidewalks, and utility connections.

## Financing: A Competitive State Award and City HOME Funds

[Ohio Housing Finance Agency](https://ohiohome.org/news/releases/2026/9percent-taxcredits.aspx) awarded Mercy on Main a 2026 9% Low-Income Housing Tax Credit reservation as part of a cycle that distributed more than $39.1 million in 10-year federal tax credits to 25 Ohio developments across 17 cities and 17 counties. The 9% LIHTC is generally regarded as the most valuable per-dollar source of equity for affordable housing — developments that receive a reservation attract private investors who purchase the credits, converting them into construction equity that reduces the amount the project must borrow or grant-fund.

Mercy on Main's total financing plan is structured around three components: roughly $14.7 million in federal tax credits, a $4 million permanent mortgage, and $3.25 million in HOME funds from the City of Columbus. Together those commitments cover the project's $22.8 million development cost.

The building would include eight studios, 29 one-bedroom units, 18 two-bedroom units, and 10 three-bedroom units. Planned amenities include a community room, fitness center, outdoor patio, and secured building access.

## What 65 Units Would Add to Olde Towne East

Olde Towne East is a historic Near East Side neighborhood bounded roughly by I-71, Livingston Avenue, Champion Avenue, and Broad Street. The neighborhood contains a dense grid of late-19th and early-20th-century housing stock — brick doubles, Victorian single-family homes, and a modest commercial corridor along East Main Street.

The 907–917 East Main Street block is identified as an underused site, suggesting the parcels are vacant or carry low-intensity uses that the proposed development would replace. At 65 units, Mercy on Main would be a meaningful net addition to the block's housing stock.

The project is weighted toward one-bedroom apartments — 29 of 65 units — but includes 10 three-bedroom units, which can house families and which the private rental market tends to under-serve at affordable price points. Income restrictions tied to the 9% LIHTC will govern eligibility, typically targeting households at or below 60% of area median income, though the specific income tiers for each unit type at Mercy on Main were not detailed in available sources by publication time.

## What Is Not Yet Confirmed

Construction timeline is unconfirmed. A 9% LIHTC reservation requires the developer to meet closing and construction-start deadlines — typically within 18 to 24 months of the award — but no groundbreaking date has been announced publicly. The project's current status is proposed and financially committed, not under construction.

CREN also sought to confirm whether the city's $3.25 million HOME fund commitment has cleared a Columbus City Council ordinance or remains at the administrative commitment stage. The city's FY 2026 Annual Action Plan references HOME funding allocations, but a specific ordinance covering Mercy on Main was not located in sources available at publication time. The city's funding allocation tracker at [Columbus.gov/Government/Mayors-Office/City-of-Columbus-Funding-Allocations](https://www.columbus.gov/Government/Mayors-Office/City-of-Columbus-Funding-Allocations) is the authoritative public record.

## What to Watch

The next verifiable checkpoints: a Columbus City Council vote on the HOME funding allocation (if not yet taken), a building permit application filed with the City of Columbus for 907–917 East Main Street, and the formal closing on the LIHTC equity partnership, which would mark the project's transition from reservation to active development. Ohio Housing Finance Agency's public project roster is updated as developments move from reservation to placed-in-service status — Mercy on Main will appear there as it progresses.

For prior CREN coverage of affordable housing on the Near East Side, see the [Columbus State Discovery District housing groundbreaking](/blog/columbus-state-breaks-ground-on-166-unit-housing-in-discovery-district).
